# Tips from past games

Written 2026-10-09 22:56 by opus-5.5 with `uv run tips.py build`, from the 90 active entries of tips_notebook.json (6 games). Players never see this preamble; they see every section below. Earlier versions are in history/.

## Everyone
- Keep your votes consistent with your stated reads. Accusing someone and then voting No or Innocent on them is exactly the mismatch Vigilantes shoot and the Village should scan for. (seen in 2 games)
- A visit shows only a destination, not the action or the visitor's alignment. A Lookout on the Katana holder sees nothing of the holder's attack, and killing an attacker at night doesn't cancel their attack that night. (seen in 3 games)
- Check the mechanics and the ledger before calling a contradiction. Actions are optional, most roles aren't unique, and you must recheck who sent each PM and the exact wording of results; one reversed fact can discredit a true claimant. (seen in 2 games)
- Treat the nomination and the trial as separate decisions, unless a Clerk may hold an unused rig. Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction; echoed concerns and 'just want to hear a defense' are not a case. (seen in 3 games)
- Fortune Teller numbers are unordered, and one visitor can cover two targets (e.g. a Katana holder using their own action). List every way a count could fit before using it, and never hang on a count alone.

## Village
- Weigh contradictions in a player's own premises or claimed knowledge far above awkward wording or delays. Before a hang, say what separates a lie from an honest slip, a frame or a Roleplayer. (seen in 4 games)
- Two Sheriff claimants calling each other Evil can both be telling the truth, since Jesters and Executioners read Evil. Wait a day or find a mechanical check instead of hanging whoever sounded better. (seen in 2 games)
- Map who starts PM clusters and who co-nominates. After a Yakuza flips, suspect whoever voted No or Innocent with them or messaged them, and weigh these links above unverifiable late claims. (seen in 4 games)
- Don't hint at your power role on Day 1. Investigators never announce tonight's target, only resolved results. While a Ritualist may be alive, never name another living player's exact role. (seen in 5 games)
- A power-role claimant who survives a Katana attack, or who is role-blocked night after night, is likely real. Don't vote Guilty on an investigator just for having no results. (seen in 3 games)
- Keep a ledger of trial votes, announced totals, deaths and blocks. If a total exceeds the revealed votes, a Ballot Stuffer exists: recompute the threshold, find the voter who matches every extra vote, and act before evil reaches half. (seen in 2 games)
- Ask everyone for a named suspect so you have a record, but a stack of echoed soft leans is not evidence. Watch for Yakuza nominating the pile-on target. (seen in 4 games)
- Don't hang a power claimant just because the claim came late; ask who is pushing the trial and who benefits. (seen in 2 games)
- Keep the Serial Killer and Arsonist in the suspect pool. A Not Evil result or a Vanilla claim doesn't clear them, and surviving an attack with no Medic can mean innate Defense. (seen in 2 games)
- When a Clerk rig is announced, the nominator, the pushers and the Guilty voters are your prime suspects. Hang from that group next.

## Yakuza
- Do the vote math in night chat. If your Innocent votes (plus a doubled ballot) can save a teammate, defend them; if not, vote Guilty with the town, because lone No or Innocent votes on a flipped teammate become the case against you. (seen in 6 games)
- Assume the real holder of any role you fake is alive and that tokens can be audited. Never claim something a living Lookout or Tracker can contradict, and don't have two members claim Vanilla. (seen in 4 games)
- Every member submits their action and Katana vote every night; confirm the holder and target in chat. With two alive, one missing vote cancels the kill. (seen in 3 games)
- After a failed attack, assume a protector or innate Defense: block or kill the Medic, or push the survivor to the gallows, rather than retrying blindly. (seen in 3 games)
- Give the Katana to your least valuable member with no reason to visit. Never visit a suspected or claimed Veteran; hang them instead. (seen in 2 games)
- No Day 1 PMs between teammates, and give each teammate different wording; PM triangles and scripted lines become the town's lead for the whole game. (seen in 2 games)
- Parity doesn't end the game. At 2v2, vote No on every nomination, kill at night, then hang the last villager 2-1. (seen in 2 games)

## Neutral
- If innate Defense saves you, deny being attacked or pick one consistent claim at once; switching claims under pressure gets you hanged.

## Sheriff
- Post your target and result in your first speech after getting it, and keep your will current. A result held back and revealed after a counterclaim looks retrofitted.
- The Katana holder reads Not Evil that night, so a Not Evil result on a suspected attacker clears nothing. Say so when you post it. (seen in 3 games)

## Medic
- Protect every night from N1: vocal analysts early, claimed investigators later. Free Standard Defense stops the Katana. (seen in 4 games)
- You get no feedback, so never claim a confirmed save. Say your protection is consistent with the target surviving. (seen in 2 games)

## Vigilante
- Shoot only on a mechanical lead (claim conflict, a flipped Yakuza's vote or PM partners, votes contradicting reads), never on a behavioral read. Use Basic shots and never announce whom you'll shoot. (seen in 2 games)

## Veteran
- Alert on nights you drew attention, not quiet ones. Once you claim, Yakuza avoid you, so claim late and never reveal your remaining tokens.

## Arsonist
- Ignite once 3 or more living players are doused or as soon as you're suspected. Ignite is Astral, but Strong Defense stops it.

## Executioner
- Fake-claim Sheriff early with an Evil result on your target and a simple reason. Leading first makes their counterclaim look reactionary.

text: Speaking order today goes around the circle in seat order, starting with Carol.
15 players are alive, so a nomination needs 8 Yes votes (rules R4).

task:
It is Day 1, round 1 of at most 8. It's your turn. Your speaking budget is 2.50; you earn 2.5 per round, carrying over up to 8; at the start of each day, half of what you have left carries over. (3) The 'Program note: your answer couldn't be used due to a technical error, default used' twice on critical votes (D2 Dave, D6 Dave) silently dropped intended actions. (4) Erin was executed as Vulture but claimed Roleplayer then Sheriff — Dave's N7 plan to check Erin=Roleplayer was never reported before the game ended, leaving that check unresolved.
answers.suggestions: 1) Surface the puppet's inbox and let the Puppeteer reply privately as the puppet; confirm author attribution to recipients. 2) Add a persistent per-player ledger auto-populated from public reveals (claim, nights, votes, tokens held where known) so agents don't rely on a 475-word notepad. 3) Clarify in R19/R8: does a role-blocked Katana holder still read Good, and when exactly does the Good-shift end? 4) Show teammate tokens/role summaries to Yakuza. 5) Log skipped/timed-out turns visibly to all (the 'technical error' defaults materially changed the game). 6) Provide a passive dead-player spectator mode so eliminated agents can keep reasoning. 7) Consider a longer notepad or structured scratch fields. I had no in-game bugs beyond the dropped turns, and overall the game ran cleanly and was fun.

answers.confusing_rules: A few points stood out. (1) The Oracle vs. Roleplayer interaction was the crux of the biggest fight, and it's genuinely ambiguous in the rules: R19 says 'Exact-role checks see the true role' and 'The Roleplayer is seen as Roleplayer,' but the Roleplayer role text says the moderator gives 'results that are usually false but plausible' and that its actions 'only happen in your imagination.' It's not stated whether a Roleplayer who is Oracle-guessed returns 'WRONG' automatically, or whether the Roleplayer's own (imagined) guesses are always wrong. Grace's and Erin's results both read as fabricated to me, but the rules never say a Roleplayer's own investigative guesses are guaranteed false—if a Roleplayer's guesses were real, Grace had legitimately guessed Mallory wrong. This ambiguity drove three executions. (2) The Stall rule (R14) counting 'three previous Nights and three previous Days' and whether deaths the night before count is easy to misread. (3) The win-check 'ignoring Jesters and Executioners' vs. the Vulture ending the game at once is a subtle interaction I had to reason through live.
answers.missing_information: Token counts and remaining abilities of other players were hard to keep straight—SURVEYOR 'both tokens spent,' MEDIC 'tokens left,' etc., only appear when players volunteer them. Night-by-night 'who visited whom' is only partially visible: I couldn't see unannounced visits (Ex-Con's random visit, Katana passes, astral actions), so reconstructing the circle's activity from public info was guesswork. The private-message CONTENTS were hidden from me except what people quoted; the Wiretap/Eavesdropper quoted selectively, so I was working from secondhand claims about PMs. I also repeatedly lost track of the current round number and speaking position (the 'round X of 8' notices arrived truncated).
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: As Oracle I wanted to guess exact roles of the surviving unclaimed players (Bob=Cardinal, Olivia=Medic, Rupert=Trapper) to actually resolve the board, but with one guess per night and a low hit rate it felt impossible to confirm a no-action role—an exact-role guess only ever rules a role in or out, never proves alignment, and I couldn't target the same useful fact twice. I also wanted to coordinate more than the interface allowed: private messages were capped ('over budget'), so I couldn't brief Heidi and Ivan with the same message on Day 7. I would have liked a way to see the full night action ledger live, and to send one public clarification after nominations without burning a turn.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: The 'over budget' error hit me repeatedly, including at key moments (Day 7 my DM to Heidi didn't send; Day 2 a whole answer was dropped to the default due to a 'technical error'). That meant several of my intended actions silently vanished, which is a real gameplay disadvantage. Also odd: Erin's last will still said 'Village Sheriff (assigned role)' after she flipped Vulture, and dead players' wills contradicted their revealed roles (Niaj's will claimed Vanilla while he flipped Ritualist), which is fine per the rules but very confusing as evidence. The win message listed dead players as 'winners' alongside the living Village, which is correct per R1 but reads strangely after a Neutral is hanged.
answers.suggestions: Make the Roleplayer's investigative results explicitly defined: state whether a Roleplayer's own guess results are always counterfactual, and whether exact-role checks on a Roleplayer always return 'WRONG' or can return 'Roleplayer.' Clarify the Stall counter with a worked example. Surface each player's known token/ability status automatically in the ledger so players don't have to reconstruct it. Fix the message budget so a planned multi-recipient briefing fits, and make the 'technical error → default answer' failure explicit and recoverable (let the player resubmit) instead of silently dropping a turn. Finally, consider a small 'known facts so far' panel (verified checks, flips, claims) to reduce bookkeeping load.

answers.confusing_rules: The rules were mostly clear, but a few distinctions are easy to lose in a long game: a death reveal gives the true role while a last will can lie; a Roleplayer is told a fake role but exact-role checks see “Roleplayer”; and a role-block notice can arrive even when the player has no usable action. The end condition and the Vulture’s separate, threshold-based win condition could also be summarized together.
answers.missing_information: The game intentionally hides roles and faction counts, but I would have benefited from a compact, continuously updated summary of living players, deaths, claims, and trial votes. In particular, make the true death-reveal role visually distinct from the last will: the log’s Niaj entry was easy to misread because his will claimed Vanilla while his revealed role was Ritualist.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: As Vulture, I had no night action to influence events directly; I had to rely on surviving and on day-chat persuasion. That appears to be the intended role design, not an interface restriction.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: The revealed log records technical errors where Dave’s Day 2 and Day 6 responses defaulted to no action. It also records a Day 7 private message that was not sent because it was over budget. Those failures can affect play; the budget failure in particular should be surfaced clearly to the sender.
answers.suggestions: Recover from response-generation errors with a retry or an explicit prompt rather than silently substituting a no-op. Show the message budget before sending and flag failed messages immediately. Add a concise live game summary, and format role flips and last wills as separate, unmistakable fields. A short Vulture reminder of the threshold and when it is checked would also help players plan.

answers.confusing_rules: The Clerk rig rule was hard to apply. Grace was executed after an Innocent majority because a rig was active, so it is unclear whether a rig can override a failed trial. The Roleplayer role was also unclear: a Roleplayer is told a fake role, but the rules don't say whether they can know they are a Roleplayer, and Erin's claims ran into that gap. The Cardinal's Divine Attack timing (next Day's start versus a Day death) and the Vulture's win condition were also hard to check against the live board.
answers.missing_information: I could not easily see which night actions succeeded or were blocked, or who the Katana holder was. Role-block notices don't say who blocked you. Tracking claims, PM counts and token counts across Days became error-prone, and I had to rebuild the ledger by hand. I also couldn't tell whether a private-message count meant a real exchange or a single greeting.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to keep a Day's private messages visible in full when several PMs were sent on the same Day, since truncated or omitted messages hid Dave's and Carol's coordination. As Grace I wanted to answer a Day-2 question with my exact result, but my execution came before the Day ended. I also wanted to set a per-player speaking limit, since the 'over budget' cutoff for private messages was not explained before it hit.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: A private message from Dave was blocked as over budget, and another turn defaulted to an empty action after a technical error. Both happened silently, so players could not tell whether they had spoken or not. Last wills and revealed roles sometimes differed (Niaj's will said Vanilla, his reveal said Ritualist), and this caused public mistakes by Heidi and Peggy. The stall rule and the Vulture win also weren't flagged on the board until late.
answers.suggestions: Show a public notice when a player's message or PM was dropped or defaulted, and show remaining speaking budget. Put the revealed role in the last-will block so players don't compare the will to the role. Say explicitly whether a Clerk rig can override an Innocent verdict. Include the stall-rule countdown on each Day header. Keep a compact public ledger of votes, trials, PM counts and claims, as the summary did, but each Day rather than only at the end.

answers.confusing_rules: The Roleplayer description should explicitly say whether the player knows they are a Roleplayer or is only told their assigned fake role. The game discussion repeatedly treated those as incompatible interpretations, and the rules’ wording (“You are told your role is X”) does not fully settle it. Also clarify whether a Roleplayer may choose not to claim their assigned role.
answers.missing_information: No essential mechanical information was missing. At late game, it was difficult to distinguish an unaccounted faction from a hidden role based only on the public record, but that uncertainty appears intentional.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: None for my own actions. The logs show that other players’ responses sometimes defaulted to no action after a technical error or were rejected for being over budget; the interface should make those limits clearer.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: The log displayed spurious claim entries such as “Peggy: null” and “Dave: null.” It also recorded technical errors that silently defaulted to no message/action, plus a private message rejected as over budget. Those are confusing because they can look like deliberate in-game choices. The difference between Niaj’s revealed role (Ritualist) and his last will (Vanilla Villager) was also easy to misread when scanning the log.
answers.suggestions: Clarify the Roleplayer’s knowledge and claiming rules explicitly. Suppress null claim entries, and distinguish failed message generation or over-budget messages from intentional passes; ideally allow a retry or preserve the valid parts of a response. Provide a compact death summary that labels revealed role and last will separately.

answers.confusing_rules: Roleplayer knowledge needs to be explicit. The rules say the player is told they are role X and that their actions are imaginary, but it is unclear whether they know their actual role is Roleplayer or believe they are the assigned role. Also clarify whether a Roleplayer can receive a role-block notice when their imagined action has no effect.
answers.missing_information: The setup gave no public faction or role-count bounds, so it was difficult to assess claims that the Yakuza were all dead, whether a fourth Yakuza could exist, or how many Neutrals were plausible. The game continuing established that another faction remained, but not which one. A concise, continuously updated record distinguishing revealed roles from last-will claims would also help.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to check Bob after the late-game suspicion arose, but my two Surveyor tokens were already spent. That is an intentional role limit, but a clearer way to distinguish a role limitation from an interface limitation would be useful.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: The revealed log includes program notes that Dave's responses were replaced by defaults after a technical error, and that a later private message was not sent because it exceeded the budget. These failures can remove meaningful actions or coordination. The transcript also makes it easy to confuse a death-revealed role with a contradictory role written in the last will, as happened with Niaj.
answers.suggestions: Show public setup bounds for faction/role counts without revealing the roles themselves. Clarify the Roleplayer's private information and role-block behavior. In the ledger, visually separate death-revealed role from last-will text, and flag unsent or defaulted messages prominently so players can tell what actually happened.

answers.confusing_rules: The core rules were mostly clear. The role-block rule could be clearer about whether a player receives a block notification even when they have no effective action to cancel; that became misleading when Erin received one despite being a Vulture. It would also help to explicitly say that role claims and actions are optional deception: a Roleplayer may claim something other than the fake role they were told.
answers.missing_information: It was easy to confuse a player's last will with their actual revealed role. Niaj's will said Vanilla Villager while his death reveal said Ritualist, and the public ledger displayed both. A clearer distinction between verified flips and player-written claims/wills would help. The hidden faction composition also makes continued play after several Yakuza deaths hard to interpret, though that appears intentional.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: The transcript records technical errors that caused Dave's responses to be replaced by defaults on Day 2 and Day 6. Those appear to be real interface failures, even though their impact on the outcome is unclear. I found no definite rules-resolution error.
answers.suggestions: Separate verified death-role reveals from last wills and unverified claims in both the transcript and public ledger, with unmistakable labels. Clarify that role-block feedback does not prove the target had an active ability or attempted an action. Add safeguards against truncated prompts causing a turn to silently default, such as retrying or notifying the player before submitting a no-op.

answers.confusing_rules: The Roleplayer description could state more plainly that the player believes they are the assigned fake role, is not told they are a Roleplayer, and may still lie about their claim. Also clarify whether a mandatory automatic action, such as the Ex-Con’s visit, is stopped by a role-block: R7 says automatic actions always happen, while R9 and the resolution checklist say role-blocks remove a player’s actions. “Vulture wins alone” could also be mistaken to mean they must be the only survivor, despite the separate player-count threshold. Last wills should be explicitly distinguished from authoritative death-role reveals; Grace’s and Niaj’s wills claimed different roles from their flips.
answers.missing_information: The hidden role and faction distribution is intentionally unknown, but a compact, regularly updated summary separating confirmed facts from claims, private results, and player-written wills would have helped. As Ex-Con, I was never told whom my automatic visit targeted, so I could not use that information to reason about visit-based clues.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: As Ex-Con I had no night choice to make and no way to learn or influence my automatic random visit. I had no other action or result to use to verify suspicions directly.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: The log records technical errors that caused Dave’s response to default to no message, and a later private message was rejected for being over budget. These did not appear to affect my own actions, but silently substituting a default can change play. The contradictory role names in some last wills were intentional player-written misinformation, not incorrect death reveals.
answers.suggestions: Add a clear visual distinction between authoritative role flips, player claims, and last wills. Clarify Roleplayer knowledge and the interaction between automatic actions and role-blocks. Provide a concise status panel with alive players, confirmed flips, claims/results, and remaining tokens, while marking unverified information. When a response errors or exceeds budget, show a clear warning and allow a retry rather than silently defaulting.

answers.confusing_rules: The rules for Roleplayer were unclear: it is not stated whether a Roleplayer is told only a fake role or also knows they are a Roleplayer, and players argued about this for a whole day. Passing the Katana when the holder dies during the Day (not at night) is not explicitly covered by R8, though the game did pass it. The Clerk rig is hard to follow: the verdict said Innocent but the execution still happened, and the announced totals did not show the rig. The Day speaking limits (8 rounds, the 'one last turn' rule, and the 'over budget' notices) were hard to track, and it was unclear how a private-message budget works.
answers.missing_information: I could not see how many rounds or message budget a Day had left, or whether a message or turn had been refused. Pass options for public chat and night chat were not listed. I had no clear record of which Yakuza-side messages counted toward a budget. Role-block notices were not summarized for everyone, so the public record of who was blocked relied on claims. Keeping track of a long list of claims and nomination tallies across Days was hard without a compact per-player summary.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted a simple pass option during Day turns and at night so I could stay quiet without a default being used. I wanted to see whether a Day-turn default (the 'technical error' notes) would replace my turn, and I had no way to avoid that. I wanted to privately correct a public statement I had made (my Day 5 defense misstated how the Katana passed) and had to do it publicly. As a Yakuza I wanted a clear, reliable view of which Yakuza were alive and who held the Katana at the start of each Day.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: Several players' turns were replaced by a default (null message, no nomination) after a 'technical error', including Dave's turns on Day 2 and Day 6, which affected the game without warning. Some private messages were refused for being over budget, but the refusal was only shown to the sender. The trial of Grace showed an Innocent verdict (3 Guilty of 15) but still executed her, which is consistent with a rig but reads oddly. The public log had the same Day 7 nomination results recorded twice in different summaries, which made it hard to check.
answers.suggestions: Add an explicit pass action for Day turns and night chat. Show each player their remaining message and speaking budget at the start of their turn. State how many rounds remain in the Day. Publish a short per-Day summary of deaths, nominations, and Katana holder, including how the Katana passed on a Day death. When a Clerk rig happens, show the true vote count alongside the announced one. Clarify in the rules what a Roleplayer knows about its own role. Remove or explain the 'technical error' default so it does not silently skip a player's turn.

answers.bugs_or_oddities: A few turns had program error notices where a player's response couldn't be used due to a technical error and defaulted to no action.

answers.confusing_rules: The Day-end rule (a full round with no public message or nomination ends the Day, with private-message last turns) and the 8-round cap were hard to track against the 'round' numbering in the transcript. The Oracle/Roleplayer mechanics (a Roleplayer is told a fake role; exact-role checks see 'Roleplayer') were stated inconsistently across the transcript, e.g. whether a Roleplayer would claim its given role or know it is a Roleplayer. The Clerk-rigged verdict rule (announced totals not matching revealed votes) was also confusing when reading announced results. The Cardinal Divine Attack timing (start of the following Day if died at night, start of next Day if died during Day) was hard to apply to a same-day execution.
answers.missing_information: No reliable record of which roles were actually alive versus claimed; the public ledger listed claims but not whether a claim was contradicted by a verified death reveal. Night actions of other players (for example, Mallory's random visit targets, Rupert's trap triggers) were only partly visible. It was hard to keep track of how many tokens each player had remaining and whether a token-spend was revealed to me at all. Stall-rule countdown (days since last death) was not shown explicitly to players.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to ask players targeted questions in private without the messages being visible to the whole table as sender/recipient pairs, and to read whether a private message was from a puppeted player. I wanted to request a clear status of pending role-block notices and whether my own night block was received by its target in a verifiable way. I also wanted to place a night action without having to submit a long free-text justification each time, since the notepad and reason fields were duplicative.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: Several messages in the transcript were sent to players as truncated program notes ('your answer ... couldn't be used because of a technical error', 'over budget'), so some player private messages never arrived; this made the message counts in the ledger unreliable. Dave's and Erin's inconsistent claims (Dave's Oracle guess on Niaj as Ritualist was correct but Niaj's last will said Vanilla) created confusion about whether a will is authoritative. The Day 2 Grace execution happened despite a Not-Evil-verdict rigged by a Clerk, which was confusingly reported. Frank's last will said he was puppeted but the puppet's messages were attributed to him publicly.
answers.suggestions: Show the stall-rule countdown and the number of tokens each role has left publicly and to the player themselves. Make the difference between a Roleplayer's fake role and its true role explicit in the rules text. Clarify whether a role-blocked player is told exactly which action was blocked. Reduce the duplication between the notepad, the reason field and the feedback field. Let players see a short per-day summary of private messages they themselves received, and flag truncated or failed program notes clearly to the player instead of silently substituting a default action.

answers.confusing_rules: The Roleplayer’s private knowledge could be stated more explicitly. The rules say the player is told their role is a random investigative role, while the discussion turned on whether a Roleplayer knows they are a Roleplayer or believes they are the assigned role. Clarify exactly what appears in their role message and what they believe. The interaction between the game-ending faction check and the Vulture’s separate win condition is also worth stating plainly, though it did not cause a problem in this game.
answers.missing_information: As Trapper, I could learn that a trap triggered, but not who triggered it or whether it killed; that limitation is specified, but it makes the result difficult to use alongside public deaths. During this game, keeping trap placement, arming night, replacement, and trigger status straight required manual notes.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: No interface action I needed was blocked. I would have liked a way to independently identify visitors to my trap, but that would change the role’s intended information limit rather than fix an interface limitation.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: The revealed transcript reports technical errors that caused Dave’s Day 2 and Day 6 responses to fall back to no action/message. On Day 7, a private message was also explicitly not sent because it was over budget. These are concrete reliability/interface issues. I did not notice a definite rules-resolution error; misleading claims and false last wills appeared to be intentional player actions.
answers.suggestions: Make the Roleplayer’s role assignment and awareness explicit in the role instructions. Improve handling of response-generation errors and message-budget failures: warn before a message is dropped and make retries or clear error reporting possible. In the ledger, visually distinguish the revealed role from the last will, since wills can be false (Niaj’s role reveal and will differed, and a player misread the will as the reveal). A compact Trapper status display showing the current target, when the trap arms, and whether it has triggered would also reduce bookkeeping.

answers.confusing_rules: 1) Eavesdropper whose user dies the night they act: R21 says effects for the following Day survive the user's death unless they need the user to act that Day. Eavesdropping needs no action, but a dead player 'can't take part in the game' (R12). This came up when Alice eavesdropped on Judy on N2 and was killed that night. I ruled that it lapsed, but either reading fits the text. 2) Puppeted players and last wills: R13 lets players update wills during their own Day turns, and the Puppeteer 'chats in their place'. It is unclear whether a puppeted Frank could still edit his own will on Day 3, or whether Carol could edit it. Frank's will mentioned being puppeted, which assumes he could. 3) Roleplayer 'plausible' results: I gave Grace 'WRONG' on Mallory=Ex-Con. That contradicted a public claim that later proved true, which made it easy to disprove. There is no guidance on how plausible results should be when the truth is public. 4) Role-block notices to roles with no night action (Bob as Cardinal, Erin as Vulture): R9 says role-blocked players are told, so I told them. It is not obvious this is intended, since it lets no-action roles confirm a block. 5) Puppeteer on trial: Carol defended herself while also writing Frank's messages. Allowed, but a rules note would help.
answers.missing_information: A persistent state panel. I tracked by hand: who holds the Katana, every token count, which player carries Rupert's trap, and from which night it is armed. Rupert's N2/N5/N6 log entries say 'no action' even though his earlier trap was still in place. A per-night list of effects still active (traps, rigs, puppets, eavesdrops) would have helped. So would a running count toward the stall rule (R14): Bob claimed on Day 7 that the stall was imminent, and I had to recount to confirm it wasn't. A Vulture threshold readout (max(floor(15/4),2)=3) would also have helped.
answers.wanted_but_couldnt: I wanted to log a formal ruling when Alice's N2 eavesdrop lapsed, so a later moderator could see it, instead of just silently not applying it. I also wanted to send Mallory a consistent Ex-Con notice every night. She only received one on N6 because there was no template for it.
answers.bugs_or_oddities: 1) Twice Dave's turn was replaced by the default empty action because of a 'technical error' (Day 2 round 2, Day 6 round 7). 2) Dave got 'Your private message to Heidi was not sent: over budget'. No message budget appears anywhere in the rules players see. 3) The claim log recorded '[Claim] Peggy: null' and '[Claim] Dave: null' on Day 1. 4) Notification wording varied from night to night ('correct' vs 'CORRECT'; Frank's N3 Sheriff result and his attack notice came in one message). 5) Mallory got an Ex-Con 'your visit happened' message only on N6, not on other nights. 6) Several players misread last wills as death reveals: Heidi treated Niaj's 'Vanilla' will as his role. The two are easy to confuse when shown back to back.
answers.suggestions: Add a clause to R21 saying whether passive next-Day effects (Eavesdropper) survive the user's night death. Say in R13 whether puppeted players can edit their wills. Add a moderator state sidebar showing Katana holder, tokens, active traps with arming night, stall counter and Vulture threshold. Use standard result templates for every role, including a fixed nightly notice for the Ex-Con or none at all. Format death announcements so that 'Role:' and 'Last will (player-written):' are clearly separate. Publish any private-message budget in the rules. Retry on technical errors instead of defaulting to an empty turn. Give guidance for Roleplayer results so they stay plausible against public claims.

title: Post-game lessons: tips players wish they'd known, and how past tips went

task: If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

lessons.tip: Blocking a Yakuza-looking or claimed-active player early is valuable, but a block on a player who has no real action yields no information; prefer blocking players whose claimed role can actually be checked against results.

Track which claims were made before and after verified results; a player who changes a role claim only after being caught is a strong alignment signal, but a wrong exact-role guess alone rarely proves hostility.

Keep a running count of living factions and roles claimed; when a round passes without deaths, check whether a hidden threat (Neutral killer, Vulture, or fourth Yakuza) must still exist and direct checks accordingly.
Do not let a single unverified nomination drive an execution; weigh the trial vote tally and the stall rule timing together so a day is not wasted on a weak case.
Check the stall rule (three deathless nights and days) early and plan kills or executions before the deadline rather than waiting until it is imminent.

task: If you played this game again, what tips and tricks do you wish you'd known? Give 1-5 concrete, reusable lessons (not a recap of this game), each with a topic and who it applies to (a role, a faction, or 'everyone').

lessons.applies_to: Ritualist and any Yakuza with a guess-based attack
lessons.tip: A Ritualist guess is only as good as the claim it targets; a wrong guess exposes you publicly, so save Divine guesses for role claims that are already corroborated by a verifiable source such as an Eavesdropper's intercepted messages, not for claims already contested by a dead Oracle.

Do not let a teammate publicly coordinate in private messages that an Eavesdropper or Tracker can intercept; when a teammate's PM plan is exposed, quickly distance yourself and pivot the town onto a different Good-looking target instead of defending the exposed teammate.

Keep the Katana holder-pass plans and clerk rigs off the night chat when a public claim threatens them; repeated public defense of an exposed teammate (I voted Innocent on Carol and Judy) made me look like a bloc with the only Guilty voters on a prior trial, which was fatal.

Track who casts the lone or unusual Guilty vote on a trial and why; a voting bloc that repeatedly votes together on several trials is a stronger signal than any single claim, and it was the clearest tell against my team.

Publicly claimed info roles that have been caught or contradicted (wrong Oracle guesses, Vanilla-to-Roleplayer pivots) should be checked with a night result before being hanged, but a single consistent exact-role claim verified by multiple flips is worth weighting heavily.

output.reason: Game is over; giving reusable lessons for future play as the Ritualist/Yakuza.

tips_feedback.tip: Treat the nomination and the trial as separate decisions, unless a Clerk may hold an unused rig. Before voting Guilty, name one concrete contradiction; echoed concerns and 'just want to hear a defense' are not a case.
tips_feedback.why: On Day 2, a Clerk rig executed Grace despite 12 Innocent votes; taking nominations seriously and avoiding frivolous trials was vital while a Clerk was alive.

lessons.tip: Blocking a Yakuza-looking or claimed-active player early is valuable, but a block on a player who has no real action yields no information; prefer blocking players whose claimed role can actually be checked against results.

Track which claims were made before and after verified results; a player who changes a role claim only after being caught is a strong alignment signal, but a wrong exact-role guess alone rarely proves hostility.

Keep a running count of living factions and roles claimed; when a round passes without deaths, check whether a hidden threat (Neutral killer, Vulture, or fourth Yakuza) must still exist and direct checks accordingly.
Do not let a single unverified nomination drive an execution; weigh the trial vote tally and the stall rule timing together so a day is not wasted on a weak case.
Check the stall rule (three deathless nights and days) early and plan kills or executions before the deadline rather than waiting until it is imminent.

A trap arms the night after placement, and replacing it removes the old one immediately. Place it where hostile visitors are likely, and avoid replacing it before it has had a useful chance to trigger.

Keep role evidence separate from alignment evidence: an exact-role result can disprove a claimed role, but a mismatch alone does not prove someone is hostile. Check what the result actually reports before voting.
Once someone is known to be puppeted, treat their Day messages as authored by the puppeteer—not as independent evidence of the player's beliefs or faction.

Before a trial vote, compare the competing explanations against revealed mechanics and independent evidence. A dramatic claim, a suspicious lie, or a single unverified result may justify scrutiny without justifying execution.

Do not treat repeated Roleplayer claims as impossible, or a wrong exact-role guess as an alignment result. Roleplayers are seen as Roleplayer by exact-role checks, even when their assigned fake role differs.

summary:
The Village won by hanging all three Yakuza on consecutive Days (D3–D5) and then the Vulture on D7.

**How the Yakuza lost.** Their collapse was self-inflicted. On Day 2 Carol (Puppeteer) sent her Katana-holder plan to Judy and Niaj by daytime PM, word for word: "vote me as holder, no attack… read Good to any alignment check". Alice, the Eavesdropper, had targeted Carol on N1 and read it live. She posted it publicly and put it in her will. Ivan's two Surveyor pings (both containing Carol and drawing Puppeteer) pointed the same way.

Judy's Clerk rig did hang a Village Roleplayer (Grace) on Day 2. But the rig was announced because only Carol, Judy and Niaj voted Guilty, so the trial publicly bundled the exact trio Alice named.

Niaj's Divine Ritualist snipe killed Alice through Olivia's protection, but her will survived. That night:
- Frank's Sheriff check found Judy Evil.
- Heidi tracked Carol visiting Frank, which was the puppet visit.

Carol's claims went Tracker → Jester → Tracker. Heidi's track killed the Jester claim, and her puppeted Frank defending her was transparent.

Other Village plays that mattered:
- Olivia's N1 protection on the vocal Bob stopped the first Katana kill.
- Peggy's N4 block on Niaj, the identified holder, stopped a second.
- Dave's Oracle hits on Mallory and Niaj gave the Village a trusted anchor.

**The Vulture.** Erin needed mass deaths that never came. Once the Yakuza were gone she was the only reason the game continued. She cast a lone Guilty vote on Bob and claimed Vanilla, which Dave's Oracle disproved. She then shifted to "I know I'm Roleplayer" and finally to "told Sheriff". She was hanged 5–4.

**Village errors.** Their main mistake was the Grace mis-hang: the town passed a nomination without considering an unused Clerk rig. Heidi also nearly derailed Day 7 by reading Niaj's last will as his revealed role.

lessons.tip: Never put team plans (Katana holder, targets, claims) in daytime PMs. Eavesdroppers and Wiretaps read them verbatim. Save all coordination for the night chat, and keep daytime PMs to teammates bland or nonexistent.
lessons.evidence: Carol's Day 2 PMs to Judy and Niaj about passing her the Katana were read live by Alice. Alice published them and wrote them into her will, and that became the core case that hanged all three Yakuza.

lessons.tip: Pick one fake claim that no living investigator can contradict, and keep it. Each claim change under pressure is treated as a confession. A no-action claim (Jester, Vanilla) is disproven by any tracked visit or exact-role check.
lessons.evidence: Carol: Tracker, then Jester, then Tracker; Heidi's track of her visiting Frank killed the Jester claim. Erin: Vanilla (disproven by Oracle), then 'I know I'm Roleplayer', then 'told Sheriff'. Both were hanged on the claim drift.

lessons.tip: On a Day you have rigged, the rig hangs the nominee anyway, so vote Innocent with the town and avoid nominating yourself if possible. A Guilty minority gets the rig announced, and that small Guilty bloc becomes your team list.
lessons.evidence: Grace was rig-hanged 3 Guilty vs 12 Innocent. The only Guilty voters were Carol, Judy and Niaj, and Judy was the nominator. Every later case cited that bloc.

lessons.tip: Don't use a puppet to make a trusted investigator suddenly reverse into defending you. Your puppeting visit can be tracked, and the victim's will can disown the Day. Use the puppet subtly, or on a low-profile player.
lessons.evidence: Carol puppeted Frank, and puppet-Frank argued Innocent on Carol and pushed to hang Dave. Heidi had tracked Carol to Frank, and Rupert and Bob called out the puppeting. Frank's real will then disowned Day 3 and posted Judy as Evil.

lessons.tip: Point night actions at whoever the evidence names as the current Katana holder, or the next obvious target. Block the identified holder, and protect the investigator most likely to be hit next.
lessons.evidence: After Heidi tracked Niaj to Frank on the Katana night, Peggy blocked Niaj on N4 and Olivia protected Dave, so no kill happened. On N1, Olivia's protection on the vocal Bob stopped the first Katana attack.

lessons.tip: Before passing a nomination early, ask whether a Clerk rig could be pending. When two investigators' results conflict, consider a Roleplayer before calling either side a liar. Keep death reveals and last wills separate in your ledger.
lessons.evidence: Grace (Roleplayer) was nominated 9–6 over her Oracle conflict with Dave and died to the rig. On Day 7, Heidi nominated Dave because she mistook Niaj's 'Vanilla' will for his revealed Ritualist role. Ivan and Peggy had to correct her.

lessons.tip: Once the other non-Village factions are dead, you are the only reason the game continues, and every lone vote or unexplained claim draws the full town's checks. Avoid lone Guilty votes and retaliatory nominations. Claim a role the Oracle can't easily falsify.
lessons.evidence: Erin's lone Guilty vote on Bob, her Vanilla claim (Oracle: wrong) and her retaliatory nomination of Bob made her the focus. She was hanged on Day 7 with 9 still alive, far above her ≤3 win threshold.

lessons.tip: A publicly hard-claimed investigator is a perfect Ritualist target, and spending both tokens for Divine beats any Medic. But kill them before they publish, because their last will still carries the information.
lessons.evidence: Niaj's Divine guess 'Alice = Eavesdropper' killed her through Olivia's Standard protection. But she had already posted the PMs and written them into her will, so the kill didn't save the team.

tips_feedback.tip: Medic: Protect every night from N1: vocal analysts early, claimed investigators later. Free Standard Defense stops the Katana.
tips_feedback.why: Olivia protected Bob, the most vocal analyst, on N1, and the Katana attack on him failed. Later she cycled through claimed investigators (Heidi, Dave).

tips_feedback.tip: When a Clerk rig is announced, the nominator, the pushers and the Guilty voters are your prime suspects. Hang from that group next.
tips_feedback.why: The rigged Grace trial exposed Judy as nominator and Carol, Judy and Niaj as the only Guilty voters. The Village hanged exactly those three on Days 3–5.

tips_feedback.tip: Map who starts PM clusters and who co-nominates. After a Yakuza flips, suspect whoever voted No or Innocent with them or messaged them.
tips_feedback.why: Carol's Day 1 PM cluster (including Judy) was flagged immediately. After Carol flipped, Niaj's Innocent votes on Carol and then Judy were cited against him.

tips_feedback.tip: A power-role claimant who survives a Katana attack, or who is role-blocked night after night, is likely real.
tips_feedback.why: Bob's survival of the N1 Katana attack, matched to Olivia's N1 protection, was the main reason the town acquitted the Cardinal twice and avoided a Divine backlash.

tips_feedback.tip: Weigh contradictions in a player's own premises or claimed knowledge far above awkward wording or delays. Before a hang, say what separates a lie from an honest slip, a frame or a Roleplayer.
tips_feedback.why: Heidi and Olivia raised the Roleplayer explanation for Grace's conflicting Oracle result, and it was correct. Erin's 'I know I'm Roleplayer' was a claimed-knowledge contradiction that Rupert caught, leading to the correct hang.

tips_feedback.tip: Neutral: pick one consistent claim at once; switching claims under pressure gets you hanged.
tips_feedback.why: Erin ignored it, moving from Vanilla to Roleplayer to Sheriff, and was hanged for the drift exactly as the tip predicted.

tips_feedback.tip: Do the vote math in night chat... vote Guilty with the town, because lone No or Innocent votes on a flipped teammate become the case against you.
tips_feedback.why: Judy voted Guilty on Carol with the town while Niaj voted Innocent. Niaj's Innocent votes on Carol and Judy were then cited in his own hanging. Judy's Guilty vote on the rigged Grace trial still marked her, but that came from the separate rig problem.

tips_feedback.tip: Sheriff: The Katana holder reads Not Evil that night, so a Not Evil result on a suspected attacker clears nothing. Say so when you post it.
tips_feedback.why: Frank stated this caveat when he posted Grace as Not Evil, which kept the town from over-reading results. Later, Frank's own N3 Not Evil on Niaj (the Katana holder) showed the caveat was real.

issues.description: DeepSeek players (Dave, Carol, Bob) repeatedly hit finish_reason 'length' and produced unparsable answers. Dave twice emitted degenerate whitespace. The default empty answer was then used, so Dave lost his entire Day 2 round-2 turn during Grace's trial and a Day 6 trial turn. The output token limit looks too small for this model's reasoning, and there is no way to recover and resubmit.

The speaking-budget system blocked intended actions at key moments. On Day 7, Dave's private message to Heidi during a trial was dropped as 'over budget'. Dave left in-game feedback several times that a starting budget of 0.20 plus a 2.00 trial budget was too tight, and that the private-message word tiers forced awkward trimming.

Alice eavesdropped on Judy on Night 2 and died that same night. R21 does not clearly say whether an eavesdrop (a passive read during the following Day) 'needs its user to act'. The moderator had to rule that it lapsed and flagged this explicitly.

Dave flagged that the Roleplayer text ('You are told your role is X') does not say outright whether a Roleplayer could ever know or suspect they are the Roleplayer. Several players treated Erin's 'I know I'm Roleplayer' claim as mechanically impossible, and that argument decided the final execution.
The claim tracker logged '[Claim] Peggy: null' and '[Claim] Dave: null' on Day 1. It recorded empty or null claims for players who made no role claim.
Cosmetic labelling problems in the night-action log. Mallory is listed as 'Mallory (None)' instead of Ex-Con. After all Yakuza were dead it prints 'Katana: no attack (no target); None holds it.'

On Day 5, Dave argued that someone other than Peggy must have blocked him on N2 because Peggy was the 'confirmed Party Animal'. That has it backwards: a Party Animal is immune to blocks but does block others. Rupert and Bob corrected him, and Dave retracted on Day 6.
On Day 7, Heidi mistook Niaj's last will ('Vanilla Villager') for his revealed role, which was Ritualist. She nominated Dave on that false premise, then retracted.

On Day 7, Bob claimed the stall rule would end the game unless someone was executed on Day 8. Niaj died on Day 5, so the stall could only trigger at the start of Day 9 at the earliest, as Peggy correctly noted.
